{{Short description|Electromagnetic equations describing superconductors}}
[[File:EfektMeisnera.svg|thumb|400 px|right|As a material drops below its superconducting critical temperature, magnetic fields within the material are expelled via the [[Meissner effect]]. The London equations give a quantitative explanation of this effect.]]
{{Electromagnetism|Electrodynamics}}

The '''London equations,''' developed by brothers [[Fritz London|Fritz]] and [[Heinz London]] in 1935,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=London|first1=F.|last2=London|first2=H.|author-link2=Heinz London|year=1935|title=The Electromagnetic Equations of the Supraconductor|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences|volume=149|issue=866|pages=71|bibcode=1935RSPSA.149...71L|doi=10.1098/rspa.1935.0048|author-link1=Fritz London|doi-access=free}}
</ref> are [[constitutive relation]]s for a [[superconductor]] relating its superconducting current to [[electromagnetic fields]] in and around it. Whereas [[Ohm's law]] is the simplest constitutive relation for an ordinary [[Electrical conductor|conductor]], the London equations are the simplest meaningful description of superconducting phenomena, and form the genesis of almost any modern introductory text on the subject.<ref>
{{cite book 
| author = Michael Tinkham  
| title = Introduction to Superconductivity 
| publisher = McGraw-Hill 
| year = 1996
| isbn = 0-07-064878-6}}</ref><ref>{{cite book 
| author = Neil Ashcroft 
| author-link = Neil Ashcroft 
| author2 = David Mermin 
| author2-link = David Mermin 
| title = Solid State Physics 
| publisher = Saunders College 
| year = 1976 
| isbn = 0-03-083993-9 
| page = [https://archive.org/details/solidstatephysic00ashc/page/738 738] 
| url-access = registration 
| url = https://archive.org/details/solidstatephysic00ashc/page/738 
}}</ref><ref name="Kittel">{{cite book 
| author = Charles Kittel  
| title = [[Introduction to Solid State Physics]]
| edition = 8th
| publisher = Wiley
| year = 2005
| isbn = 0-471-41526-X}}</ref> A major triumph of the equations is their ability to explain the [[Meissner effect]],<ref>{{cite journal 
|last= Meissner
|first= W.
|title=Ein neuer Effekt bei Eintritt der Supraleitfähigkeit
|author2=R. Ochsenfeld
 |journal= Naturwissenschaften
|volume= 21
|year= 1933 
|doi= 10.1007/BF01504252 
|pages= 787 |bibcode = 1933NW.....21..787M 
|issue= 44 |s2cid= 37842752
}}
</ref> wherein a material exponentially expels all internal magnetic fields as it crosses the superconducting threshold.

==Description==

There are two London equations when expressed in terms of measurable fields: 
:<math>\frac{\partial \mathbf{j}_{\rm s}}{\partial t} = \frac{n_{\rm s} e^2}{m}\mathbf{E}, \qquad \mathbf{\nabla}\times\mathbf{j}_{\rm s} =-\frac{n_{\rm s} e^2}{m }\mathbf{B}. </math>
Here <math>{\mathbf{j}}_{\rm s}</math> is the (superconducting) [[current density]], '''E''' and '''B''' are respectively the electric and magnetic fields within the superconductor, 
<math>e\,</math> <!-- do not delete "\'": It improved display of the formula in certain browsers. --->
is the charge of an electron or proton, 
<math>m\,</math> <!-- do not delete "\'": It improved display of the formula in certain browsers. --->
is electron mass, and 
<math>n_{\rm s}\,</math> <!-- do not delete "\'": It improved display of the formula in certain browsers. --->
is a phenomenological constant loosely associated with a [[number density]] of superconducting carriers.<ref name="James F. Annett 2004 58">{{cite book 
| author = James F. Annett  
| title = Superconductivity, Superfluids and Condensates 
| url = https://archive.org/details/superconductivit00anne_663
| url-access = limited
| publisher = Oxford
| year = 2004
| isbn = 0-19-850756-9
| page = [https://archive.org/details/superconductivit00anne_663/page/n60 58]}}</ref>

The two equations can be combined into a single "London Equation"
<ref name="James F. Annett 2004 58"/><ref>{{cite book 
| author = John David Jackson  
| title = Classical Electrodynamics 
| url = https://archive.org/details/classicalelectro00jack_697
| url-access = limited
| publisher = John Wiley & Sons
| year = 1999
| isbn = 0-19-850756-9
| page = [https://archive.org/details/classicalelectro00jack_697/page/n627 604]}}</ref>
in terms of a specific [[magnetic vector potential|vector potential]] <math>\mathbf{A}_{\rm s}</math> which has been [[Gauge fixing|gauge fixed]] to the "London gauge", giving:
<ref name="London 1948">{{cite journal 
|last1=London 
|first1=F. 
|title=On the Problem of the Molecular Theory of Superconductivity 
|journal=Physical Review 
|date=September 1, 1948 
|volume=74 
|issue=5 
|pages=562–573 
|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.74.562 
|bibcode=1948PhRv...74..562L 
|url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.74.562|url-access=subscription 
}}</ref>
:<math>\mathbf{j}_{\rm s} =-\frac{n_{\rm s}e^2}{m}\mathbf{A}_{\rm s}. </math>
In the London gauge, the vector potential obeys the following requirements, ensuring that it can be interpreted as a current density:<ref>
{{cite book 
| author = Michael Tinkham  
| title = Introduction to Superconductivity 
| url = https://archive.org/details/introductiontosu00tink_948
| url-access = limited
| publisher = McGraw-Hill 
| year = 1996
| isbn = 0-07-064878-6
| page = [https://archive.org/details/introductiontosu00tink_948/page/n23 6]}}</ref>

* <math> \nabla\cdot \mathbf{A}_{\rm s} = 0,</math>
* <math>\mathbf{A}_{\rm s} = 0 </math> in the superconductor bulk,
* <math>\mathbf{A}_{\rm s} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0,</math> where <math>\hat{\mathbf{n}}</math> is the [[normal vector]] at the surface of the superconductor.

The first requirement, also known as [[Gauge fixing|Coulomb gauge]] condition, leads to the constant superconducting electron density <math>\dot \rho_{\rm s} = 0</math> as expected from the continuity equation. The second requirement is consistent with the fact that supercurrent flows near the surface. The third requirement ensures no accumulation of superconducting electrons on the surface. These requirements do away with all gauge freedom and uniquely determine the vector potential. One can also write the London equation in terms of an arbitrary gauge<ref name="Bardeen 1951">{{cite journal 
|last1=Bardeen 
|first1=J. 
|title=Choice of Gauge in London's Approach to the Theory of Superconductivity 
|journal=Physical Review 
|date=February 1, 1951 
|volume=81 
|issue=3 
|pages=469–470 
|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.81.469.2 
|bibcode=1951PhRv...81..469B 
|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.81.469.2|url-access=subscription 
}}</ref> <math>\mathbf{A}</math> by simply defining <math>\mathbf{A}_{\rm s} = (\mathbf{A} + \nabla \phi)</math>, where <math>\phi</math> is a scalar function and <math>\nabla \phi</math> is the change in gauge which shifts the arbitrary gauge to the London gauge.
The vector potential expression holds for magnetic fields that vary slowly in space.<ref name="Kittel" />

==London penetration depth==
{{Main|London penetration depth}}
[[File:London-penetration.png|thumb|The magnetic field strength as a function of position at the boundary between a normal conductor and a superconductor given an external magnetic field <math>B_0</math>.]]
If the second of London's equations is manipulated by applying [[Ampere's law]],<ref>(The displacement is ignored because it is assumed that electric field only varies slowly with respect to time, and the term is already suppressed by a factor of ''c''.)</ref>
:<math>\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}</math>,
then it can be turned into the [[Helmholtz equation]] for magnetic field:
:<math>\nabla^2 \mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\rm s}^2}\mathbf{B} </math>

where the inverse of the [[Laplacian]] eigenvalue:

:<math>\lambda_{\rm s} \equiv \sqrt{\frac{m}{\mu_0 n_{\rm s} e^2}}</math>

is the characteristic length scale, <math>\lambda_{\rm s}</math>, over which external magnetic fields are exponentially suppressed: it is called the [[London penetration depth]]: typical values are from 50 to 500 [[nanometers|nm]].

For example, consider a superconductor within free space where the magnetic field outside the superconductor is a constant value pointed parallel to the superconducting boundary plane in the ''z'' direction. If ''x'' leads perpendicular to the boundary then the solution inside the superconductor may be shown to be

:<math>B_z(x) = B_0 e^{-x / \lambda_{\rm s}}. \,</math><!--- Do not delete "\'". It serves to improve the display of this equation in certain browsers --->

From here the physical meaning of the London penetration depth can perhaps most easily be discerned.

==Rationale==

===Original arguments===

While the above equations cannot be formally derived,<ref name="Michael Tinkham 1996 5">{{cite book 
| author = Michael Tinkham  
| title = Introduction to Superconductivity 
| url = https://archive.org/details/introductiontosu00tink_948
| url-access = limited
| publisher = McGraw-Hill 
| year = 1996
| isbn = 0-07-064878-6
| page = [https://archive.org/details/introductiontosu00tink_948/page/n22 5]}}</ref>
the Londons did follow a certain intuitive logic in the formulation of their theory. Substances across a stunningly wide range of composition behave roughly according to [[Ohm's law]], which states that current is proportional to electric field. However, such a linear relationship is impossible in a superconductor for, almost by definition, the electrons in a superconductor flow with no resistance whatsoever. To this end, the London brothers imagined electrons as if they were free electrons under the influence of a uniform external electric field. According to the [[Lorentz force law]] 
:<math>\mathbf{F}=m \dot{\mathbf{v}}=-e\mathbf{E} - e\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}</math>
these electrons should encounter a uniform force, and thus they should in fact accelerate uniformly. Assume that the electrons in the superconductor are now driven by an electric field, then according to the definition of current density <math>\mathbf{j}_{\rm s} = -n_{\rm s} e \mathbf{v}_{\rm s}  </math>we should have

<math>\frac{\partial \mathbf{j}_{\rm s}}{\partial t} = -n_{\rm s} e \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}_{\rm s}}{\partial t } =\frac{n_{\rm s} e^2}{m}\mathbf{E}  </math>

This is the first London equation. To obtain the second equation, take the curl of the first London equation and apply [[Faraday's law of induction|Faraday's law]],
:<math>\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}</math>,
to obtain
:<math> \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left( \nabla \times \mathbf{j}_{\rm s} + \frac{n_{\rm s} e^2}{m} \mathbf{B} \right) = 0.</math>

As it currently stands, this equation permits both constant and exponentially decaying solutions. The Londons recognized from the Meissner effect that constant nonzero solutions were nonphysical, and thus postulated that not only was the time derivative of the above expression equal to zero, but also that the expression in the parentheses must be identically zero:

<math> \nabla \times \mathbf{j}_{\rm s} + \frac{n_{\rm s} e^2}{m} \mathbf{B} = 0</math>

This results in the second London equation and  <math>\mathbf{j}_{\rm s} =-\frac{n_{\rm s}e^2}{m}\mathbf{A}_{\rm s} </math> (up to a gauge transformation which is fixed by choosing "London gauge") since the magnetic field is defined through <math> B=\nabla \times A_{\rm s}.</math>

Additionally, according to Ampere's law <math>\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}_{\rm s}</math> , one may derive that: <math>\nabla \times (\nabla\times \mathbf{B}) =\nabla \times \mu_0 \mathbf{j}_{\rm s}  =-\frac{\mu_0 n_{\rm s} e^2}{m} \mathbf{B}.  </math>

On the other hand, since <math>\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0  </math>, we have <math>\nabla \times (\nabla\times \mathbf{B}) = -\nabla^2\mathbf{B}  </math>, which leads to the spatial distribution of magnetic field obeys :

<math>\nabla^2 \mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\rm s}^2}\mathbf{B} </math>

with penetration depth <math>\lambda_{\rm s}=\sqrt{\frac{m}{\mu_0 n_{\rm s} e^2}}</math>. In one dimension, such [[Helmholtz equation]] has the solution form <math>B_z(x) = B_0 e^{-x / \lambda_{\rm s}}. \,</math>

Inside the superconductor <math>(x>0)</math>, the magnetic field exponentially decay, which well explains the Meissner effect. With the magnetic field distribution, we can use Ampere's law <math>\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}_{\rm s}</math> again to see that the supercurrent  <math>\mathbf{j}_{\rm s}</math>also flows near the surface of superconductor, as expected from the requirement for interpreting <math>\mathbf{j}_{\rm s}</math>as physical current.

While the above rationale holds for superconductor, one may also argue in the same way for a perfect conductor. However, one important fact that distinguishes the superconductor from perfect conductor is that perfect conductor does not exhibit Meissner effect for <math>T<T_c</math>. In fact, the postulation <math> \nabla \times \mathbf{j}_{\rm s} + \frac{n_{\rm s} e^2}{m} \mathbf{B} = 0</math> does not hold for a perfect conductor. Instead, the time derivative must be kept and cannot be simply removed. This results in the fact that the time derivative of <math> \mathbf{B}</math> field (instead of <math> \mathbf{B}</math> field) obeys:

<math>\nabla^2 \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\rm s}^2}\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}. </math>

For <math>T<T_c</math>, deep inside a perfect conductor we have <math>\dot \mathbf{B} = 0 </math> rather than <math>\mathbf{B}=0 </math> as the superconductor. Consequently, whether the magnetic flux inside a perfect conductor will vanish depends on the initial condition (whether it's zero-field cooled or not).

===Canonical momentum arguments===

It is also possible to justify the London equations by other means.<ref>{{cite book 
| author = John David Jackson  
| title = Classical Electrodynamics 
| url = https://archive.org/details/classicalelectro00jack_449
| url-access = limited
| publisher = John Wiley & Sons
| year = 1999
| pages = [https://archive.org/details/classicalelectro00jack_449/page/n602 603]–604
| isbn = 0-19-850756-9}}</ref><ref name="Tinkham">{{cite book 
| author = Michael Tinkham  
| title = Introduction to Superconductivity 
| url = https://archive.org/details/introductiontosu00tink_948
| url-access = limited
| publisher = McGraw-Hill 
| year = 1996
| pages = [https://archive.org/details/introductiontosu00tink_948/page/n22 5]–6
| isbn = 0-07-064878-6}}</ref>
Current density is defined according to the equation
:<math>\mathbf{j}_{\rm s} =- n_{\rm s} e \mathbf{v}_{\rm s}.</math>
Taking this expression from a classical description to a quantum mechanical one, we must replace values <math>\mathbf{j}_{\rm s} </math> and <math>\mathbf{v}_{\rm s} </math> by the expectation values of their operators. The velocity operator
:<math>\mathbf{v}_{\rm s} = \frac{1}{m} \left( \mathbf{p} + e \mathbf{A}_{\rm s} \right) </math>
is defined by dividing the gauge-invariant, kinematic momentum operator by the particle mass ''m''.<ref>{{cite book 
| author = L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz
| title = Quantum Mechanics- Non-relativistic Theory
| publisher = Butterworth-Heinemann
| year = 1977
| pages = 455–458
| isbn = 0-7506-3539-8}}</ref> Note we are using <math>-e</math> as the electron charge.
We may then make this replacement in the equation above. However, an important assumption from the [[Bcs theory|microscopic theory of superconductivity]] is that the superconducting state of a system is the ground state, and according to a theorem of Bloch's,<ref>Tinkham p.5: "This theorem is apparently unpublished, though famous."</ref>
in such a state the canonical momentum '''p''' is zero. This leaves
:<math>\mathbf{j} =-\frac{n_{\rm s}e^2}{m}\mathbf{A}_{\rm s}, </math>
which is the London equation according to the second formulation above.

==Flux quantization==
[[File:Flux-quantization-setup.png|thumb|The setup for the derivation of magnetic flux quantization, showing the external magnetic field inside the hollow superconductor and the integration contour <math>\mathcal{C}</math>.]]
The [[Magnetic flux quantum|quantization of the magnetic flux]] can be predicted using the London equations. For this, it is assumed that the density of superconducting electrons is governed by a bosonic [[wavefunction]] <math>\psi</math>, which satisfies
:<math>n_s=|\psi|^2.</math>
While the amplitude of <math>\psi</math> is fixed by the number density, its phase <math>\theta(\mathbf{r})</math> can vary over space. Thus, it is possible to write
:<math>\psi(\mathbf{r})=\sqrt{n_s} e^{i\theta(\mathbf{x})}.</math>
Using the canonical momentum, the velocity is written in terms of the wavefunction as
:<math>\mathbf{v}=\frac{1}{m}\left(-i\hbar \nabla - \frac{q}{c}\mathbf{A}\right),</math>
such that the current is
:<math>\mathbf{j}=q\psi^\dagger \mathbf{v}\psi=\frac{n_s q}{m}\left( \hbar\nabla\theta-\frac{q}{c}\mathbf{A} \right).</math>

Flux quantization can be observed in a hollow superconducting cylinder, where an external magnetic field is applied inside the hole, and the cylinder itself is free of magnetic fields and currents due to the Meissner effect, so the phase is governed by the equation
:<math>\hbar \nabla \theta - \frac{q}{c}\mathbf{A}=0,</math>
Tracing a contour <math>\mathcal{C}</math> around the hole, the first term becomes
:<math>\oint_\mathcal{C}\nabla \theta \cdot dl=\theta_2-\theta_1.</math>
For the wavefunction to be single-valued, this must be a multiple of <math>2\pi</math>.
By [[Stokes' theorem]], the second term is
:<math>\oint_\mathcal{C} \mathbf{A}\cdot dl=\int_\mathcal{C} \nabla \times \mathbf{A}\cdot d\mathbf{s}=\int_\mathcal{C}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{s}=\Phi,</math>
where <math>\Phi</math> is the magnetic flux inside the hole. Since these two terms must be equal, there is the requirement that
:<math>\Phi=n \frac{2\pi\hbar c}{q}\equiv n\Phi_0,</math>
where <math>n</math> is an integer. Thus, the magnetic flux in the hole is quantized in terms of the magnetic flux quantum <math>\Phi_0</math>.<ref name="Kittel" />{{rp|279-281}}
